newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Mladic gives up leadership of Bosnian Serb army.
newsitem.headline: Mladic gives up leadership of Bosnian Serb army.

text.p: General Ratko Mladic formally gave up leadership of the Bosnian Serb Army on Thursday, ending a power struggle that threatened to lead to civil war.
Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic presided over the hastily organised ceremony, which was arranged after Mladic, an indicted war criminal, agreed to quit late on Wednesday.
Mladic wrote to the civilian leadership in the Serb "capital" of Pale to confirm that he had authorised his deputy, General Manojlo Milovanovic to briefly assume command.
Milovanovic's only task was to attend the ceremony where he transfered power to General Pero Colic, who has the support of the civilian leadership.

Sitting between the two generals, Plavsic thanked Mladic for leading the Bosnian Serb Army through the 1992-95 war against Bosnia's mainly Moslem government, only hinting at the bitter dispute between civilians and military.
"I have verified this transfer of duties," she said. "Perhaps it lasted a little bit long, but since a complex structure is involved, it took a bit long."
The delay centred on the refusal of Mladic, 52, and his staff to accept their effective dismissal by Plavsic.
She replaced Mladic with the relatively unknown Colic, but Mladic refused to recognise their demotion and occupied the military headquarters in Han Pijesak.
In his letter of resignation, Mladic set conditions aimed at protecting staff who had remained loyal to him.
He asked for guarantees that "the continuity of the Bosnian Serb Army will be ensured", serving soldiers could chose their futures and that families would be cared for.
He also demanded guarantees no inquiry would be launched against any soldier who acted on his orders and that no action would be taken against any of them.
Mladic's capitulation is a victory for rival and fellow indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic, formerly Bosnian Serb president and guiding hand behind Plavsic's government.
Karadzic tried and failed to sack Mladic last year over the general's allegations political leaders were corrupt.

Karadzic and Mladic are both wanted by the United Nations international war crimes tribunal in The Hague but little has been done to arrest them and the Bosnian Serbs are unlikely to agree to either being extradited to The Hague.

Mladic, a hero to ordinary Bosnian Serbs, has been charged with genocide and crimes against humanity for his role in the siege of Sarajevo and the massacre of about 8,000 unarmed Moslems from the eastern Bosnian town of Srebrenica.

The Dayton peace accord which ended Bosnia's 3-1/2 year war, bars any person indicted for war crimes from holding office and Mladic's continued role as head of the Bosnian Serb Army was a constant irritation to the international community.
Mladic is expected to stay in Bosnia because analysts say no neighbouring state, including Yugoslavia, will pay the price of harbouring one of the world's most wanted men.
